newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Vote clears way for Australia's largest bank merger.
newsitem.headline: Vote clears way for Australia's largest bank merger.

text.p: Advance Bank shareholders cleared the way for Australia's largest bank merger on Monday when they approved a scheme for St George Bank to make a cash and scrip offer worth A$2.65 billion (US$2.1 billion).
Advance said polling showed nearly 90 percent of voting shareholders were in favour of the scheme which required a 75 percent margin to win approval.

The merger of the two Sydney-based regional banks would create Australia's fifth largest bank, with assets of A$40 billion and a market capitalisation of A$4.5 billion, making it one of Australia's top 25 listed companies.

Under the deal, Advance shareholders would be offered a combination of A$2.10 in cash, a 20 cent special cash dividend and new St George shares up to a value of A$5.00 per Advance share, giving a total value of about A$7.30.
The deal now requires the clearance of the Supreme Court of New South Wales on January 6 and two further procedural meetings for the Trustees of Advance's non-participating stock.
Asked if he was confident the deal would be successfully completed, a cautious St George chief, Jim Sweeney said: "I'm as confident as I can be. It's the first step in the dance".
Sweeney has reason to be cautious. St George has had five unsuccessful merger attempts in the past two years.

Most recently, St George's bid for Queensland-based regional bank, Metway, was scuttled by the Queensland government, which offered a higher bid through its wholly-owned financial services group Suncorp and the Queensland Industry and Development Corp.
Last year, St George was foiled in its merger bid with Perth-based Challenge Bank when Westpac Banking Corp made a higher offer.

Analysts said St George's eagerness to merge has been spurred by Australia's largest bank, National Australia Bank, which has been sniffing at St George's register since February and currently holds a 6.8 percent stake.

NAB, which last week revealed a three percent stake in Advance, has been seen as a possible blocker of the merger with analysts saying it was keen to put the deal on ice until an inquiry into the finance and banking sector reports in March.
The latest merger plan sees Advance required to pay St George A$100 million if it was taken over by a third party.
Although St George's reaction to the approval was cautious, the market was more confident with the consequences reflected in the share prices of the players involved.
"The approval appears to clinch the deal for St George and although this was bad for its shares, it was good for Advance and National Australia Bank stock," a Sydney based dealer said.
St George stock slumped 19 cents to A$7.88 on Monday while Advance shares rose 16 cents to A$6.90 and NAB shares advanced 14 cents to A$14.63.
